name: Pea shoots
summary: Sweet, crunchy shoots that taste like fresh peas. Big yields and easy for a first tray.
problems: Seeds that sit too wet can sour; drain well after soaking. Tall shoots can flop without enough light.
notes: A tray gives roughly 250 to 350 g (9 to 12 oz). Cut above the lowest leaves and a tray often regrows once. Goats and chickens both like pea shoots. Start with a little and add more over a week or two: lush legume greens can cause bloat in goats. Check with your vet before making it a regular feed.

name: Sunflower microgreens
summary: Thick, nutty, crunchy greens. Many growers' favorite.
problems: Seed hulls stick to the leaves; mist and brush them off, or keep the blackout cover on a day longer. Use black oil sunflower seed sold for sprouting.
notes: A tray gives roughly 300 to 400 g (11 to 14 oz). Harvest before the first true leaves appear, or they turn bitter. A good treat for chickens and goats. Start with a little and add more over a week or two. Check with your vet before making it a regular feed.

name: Radish microgreens
summary: Spicy, fast greens ready in about a week. Pink-stemmed kinds are pretty on a plate.
problems: Fine white root hairs are normal and often mistaken for mold.
notes: A tray gives roughly 200 to 300 g (7 to 11 oz). Radish is a cabbage-family plant: offer animals only a small handful now and then. Check with your vet before making it a regular feed.

name: Broccoli microgreens
summary: Mild, slightly peppery greens, one of the most popular for salads and sandwiches.
problems: Thick sowing in still air can mold; keep a fan running.
notes: A tray gives roughly 150 to 250 g (5 to 9 oz). Cabbage-family greens are fine for animals as a small treat, not a main feed. Check with your vet before making it a regular feed.

name: Kale microgreens
summary: Mild cabbage flavor and soft leaves. Grows like broccoli microgreens.
problems: Same as broccoli: give it moving air and water from below.
notes: A tray gives roughly 150 to 250 g (5 to 9 oz). For animals, a small treat only, as with other cabbage-family plants. Check with your vet before making it a regular feed.

name: Mustard microgreens
summary: Hot, sharp little greens that wake up a sandwich. Red and green kinds.
problems: Very fine seed; sow it evenly so patches don't get crowded and mold.
notes: A tray gives roughly 100 to 200 g (4 to 7 oz). Mustard is strong and can upset animals' stomachs, so keep it for people.

name: Arugula microgreens
summary: Peppery and nutty, a stronger taste than the size suggests.
problems: Slow and uneven to sprout if the mix dries out in the first days.
notes: A tray gives roughly 100 to 150 g (4 to 5 oz). A cabbage-family plant: only a small handful for animals. Check with your vet before making it a regular feed.

name: Red cabbage microgreens
summary: Purple stems and blue-green leaves with a mild cabbage taste.
problems: Same care as broccoli. Stems are purpler with good light.
notes: A tray gives roughly 150 to 250 g (5 to 9 oz). A small treat only for animals, like other cabbage-family greens. Check with your vet before making it a regular feed.

name: Beet microgreens
summary: Bright red stems and an earthy, sweet taste. Slower than most.
problems: Seed caps stick to the leaves. Sprouting is uneven; keep the blackout cover on until most have come up.
notes: A tray gives roughly 100 to 200 g (4 to 7 oz). Beet greens are high in oxalates, so animals should get only a little. Check with your vet before making it a regular feed.

name: Amaranth microgreens
summary: Tiny, brilliant magenta greens with a mild, earthy taste.
problems: Delicate and slow at first. Likes warmth, around 24 °C (75 °F). Water gently from below so the stems don't fall over.
notes: A tray gives roughly 50 to 100 g (2 to 4 oz). Amaranth greens can hold oxalates and nitrates, so give animals only a little. Check with your vet before making it a regular feed.

name: Basil microgreens
summary: Little leaves with full basil flavor. Slower to grow, but worth it for cooking.
problems: The seeds turn jelly-like when wet; don't soak them, just sow on damp mix and mist. Needs warmth.
notes: A tray gives roughly 50 to 100 g (2 to 4 oz). Basil is fine for animals in small amounts. Check with your vet before making it a regular feed.

name: Buckwheat microgreens
summary: Tender, lemony greens on pink stems. Fast and easy for people.
problems: Grows tall fast; cut before the leaves get tough.
notes: A tray gives roughly 250 to 350 g (9 to 12 oz). Buckwheat greens can make animals sensitive to sunlight, so keep them for people.

name: Wheatgrass
summary: Young wheat blades, juiced for people or fed fresh to animals.
problems: Mold at the base comes from too much water and still air. Rinse soaked seed well.
notes: A tray gives roughly 300 to 450 g (11 to 16 oz). Goats and chickens eat it readily. Start with a little and add more over a week or two so their stomachs adjust. Check with your vet before making it a regular feed.

name: Barley fodder
summary: A thick mat of sprouted barley, roots and all, grown as fresh green feed for animals.
problems: Mold is the main risk: rinse soaked seed, water often with clean water, drain well and keep air moving. Never feed moldy fodder.
notes: A tray grows into a mat several times the weight of the seed. Feed the whole mat, roots too. Fodder is a supplement, not a full diet: keep giving hay. Start with a little and add more over a week or two. Check with your vet before making it a regular feed.

name: Garden cress
summary: Peppery, quick greens that grow on almost anything, even a damp paper towel.
problems: Seeds turn sticky when wet; sow them dry on damp mix and mist. Don't soak.
notes: A tray gives roughly 100 to 200 g (4 to 7 oz). A cabbage-family plant, so only a small handful for animals. Check with your vet before making it a regular feed.
